summary: This informational document describes the process and results of a statistical analysis of WHOIS output objects collected from Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries. It helps show what WHOIS data looks like in practice.

eli5.summary: Researchers collected lots of WHOIS answers and counted what they contained. This reports what they found.

questions: what fields are in whois output
how many registries were surveyed for whois
subtitle: A survey of what registry WHOIS servers actually return, done to feed the design of RDAP.

tldr.problem: WHOIS has no standard query or response format, so every registry reports registration data with different fields and labels, which made it hard to design a single replacement data model.
tldr.mechanism: The authors collected WHOIS output from the five Regional Internet Registries and from 124 domain registries (106 ccTLDs and 18 gTLDs) and compared which data elements exist and what each registry calls them.
tldr.outcome: The inventory showed that few elements are supported everywhere and that most have many labels. It became input to the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) specifications.

today: RFC 7485 is an Informational document and the data does not list any RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a snapshot of WHOIS practice from July 2012, and the RDAP specifications RFC 7480, RFC 7482, RFC 7483 and RFC 7484 were developed using it as input.

sections.title: Why Inventory WHOIS
sections.content:
Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) and Domain Name Registries (DNRs) have long offered a public lookup of part of their databases, mostly through the WHOIS protocol (RFC 3912). The RFC lists three shortcomings: WHOIS has no query and response format, no user authentication or access control for differentiated access, and no internationalization, so it does not consistently support Internationalized Domain Names.

This document records an inventory of registry data objects. The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP, RFC 7480, RFC 7482, RFC 7483 and RFC 7484) was developed using the inventory as input. It does not try to analyze every query and response type, only the most common objects.
sections.eli5: The old lookup service answers however it likes. Before building a better one, the authors wrote down all the different ways people answer today.

sections.title: How the Data Was Collected
sections.content:
WHOIS data, both port 43 responses and web responses, was collected between July 9, 2012, and July 20, 2012. For the number space, the authors queried the WHOIS servers of the five RIRs (AFRINIC, APNIC, ARIN, LACNIC and RIPE NCC) for IP addresses, ASNs, contacts and organizations, and then grouped elements that mean the same thing but use different labels.

For domains, a script queried 294 ccTLDs using the string nic.ccTLD. Responses came from 106 ccTLDs. Adding 18 gTLDs, whose data came from their contracts with ICANN, gave a sample of 124 registries. Web WHOIS data was collected manually from those 124. Data for the top 10 ccTLD registries was re-verified with other domain names. Objects defined by the gTLD applicant guidebook and by EPP are called public objects; privately specified ones are other objects.
sections.eli5: The researchers asked 124 registries the same kind of question, wrote down every answer and sorted answers that meant the same thing into piles.

sections.title: What the Five RIRs Return
sections.content:
All five RIRs provide information on IP addresses, ASNs and contacts, but each uses its own data model. The document tabulates the organization, contact, IP address and ASN objects. Some elements are not supported by every RIR, some get different labels from different RIRs, and in some cases the same label is used for different elements by different RIRs.

For example, the organization name is organisation at AFRINIC, Name at ARIN, Owner at LACNIC and org-name at RIPE NCC, and the table marks APNIC as NA. The conclusion is that a selection of the most common and useful fields was made to build a single data model for each object, and that initial selection was the starting point for RFC 7483.
sections.eli5: Five libraries each file their books with different labels. Before making one shared catalog, you first have to see which labels each library uses.

sections.title: What the Domain Registries Return
sections.content:
All 124 registries support domain queries. Eight ccTLDs and 15 gTLDs support queries for specific contacts, 10 ccTLDs and 18 gTLDs support nameserver queries, and four ccTLDs and 18 gTLDs support registrar queries. Domain WHOIS data contains 68 data elements that use 550 labels in total, plus 392 other objects.

Support is uneven. 95.16% of the 124 registries have a Domain Name element and 85.48% a Creation Date, but only 11.29% report DNSSEC and 3.23% a Last Transferred Date. Among contacts, only Registrant Name and Admin Street are supported by more than half of registries, and no tech or billing element is. Nameservers use 63 different labels, partly because some registries number them ("nameserver 1" to "nameserver n"). Two presentation styles are common, key-value and data block, and 11 registries answer in a local script rather than English.
sections.eli5: Almost every registry says the name of the website. Only a few say whether it has a safety lock, and most call the same thing by a different word.

sections.title: Findings and Limitations
sections.content:
A cumulative analysis found that about 5% of the data elements are supported by 111 registries (90%), while about 90% of the elements are supported by only 14 registries (11%). Around 90% of data elements have more than two labels, so the authors conclude that a standard, unified format for object names in a WHOIS response is necessary. Because of the many private objects, an IANA registry is advised to keep JSON names unique in RDAP.

The survey lists its own limits. Querying nic.ccTLD may return customized data, the script was anonymous so only public data was seen, the 11 non-English responses may be misclassified, extension elements are used randomly, and the samples for contact, nameserver and registrar queries are small.
sections.eli5: The count showed that only a few boxes appear on every form, and that most boxes have lots of names. The authors also admit where their counting might be off.

sections.title: Reference Extension Objects
sections.content:
Some objects exist in WHOIS today but are not covered by RFC 7483. The document lists them as reference extension objects for discussion. For RIRs these are company, maintainer, list of resources and referral NOC contact. For DNRs, chosen from the top 50 other objects supported by more than five registries, they are zone-c, maintainer, Registration URL, anonymous, hold, nsl-id, obsoleted and Customer Service Contact.

The Security Considerations section says only that the document provides no security services and adds nothing beyond what RFC 7481 discusses.
sections.eli5: A few extra boxes did not make it onto the new shared form. The authors list them in case people want to add them later.
